title: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (1 of 7)
hook: so, what do you do? the third path asks a harder question
tomorrow: Jnana yoga: neti neti in practice; Shankara's method; the Ashtavakra Gita opening (2 of 7)

segments.voice: Last week: bhakti yoga, and the line love as the road. Nine doors, the Tamil saints, Mira, Tulsidas, Surdas, and a street full of kirtan. Today, the third path.

You're at a party, and someone you've just met asks the question. So, what do you do? You answer: a job title, maybe where you live, whether you have kids, what you studied. Now imagine they don't accept any of it. No, not your job. Who are you? You try your name. That's a label your parents picked. Your personality? That's changed a lot since you were eight. Your body? Most of it has been rebuilt since you were a child. Keep going, and it gets strange fast. The third path of yoga starts right there, at the question you can't quite answer.
screen: `SO, WHAT DO YOU DO?` → `NO: WHO ARE YOU?` → `THE QUESTION YOU CAN'T ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Jnana comes from the Sanskrit root jna, to know. It's a cousin of the English word know, and the Greek gnosis. But jnana doesn't mean information. You can't look it up. It means knowing the way you know you're awake: direct, from the inside. Karma yoga asked what you do. Bhakti asked who you love. Jnana asks who is doing and loving in the first place. One of the oldest teachers of this road is a sage in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad named Yajnavalkya, and he gives it a two-word tool. Neti, neti. Not this, not this. Asked to describe the self, the real I, he refused to give it a label. Whatever you can point at is not it. Not the body. Not the breath. Not the thoughts, not the feelings. It sounds like a riddle, but the logic is simple. Anything you can observe is something you're observing, so it can't be the observer. Elsewhere in the same Upanishad, Yajnavalkya asks: by what would one know the knower? Your eye can see everything except itself. So the jnana path isn't adding knowledge. It's subtraction: peeling off everything that turns out to be an object, until what's left is the one who was looking all along. This week: practicing that peeling, the method of the great teacher Shankara, and a strange, fierce little book called the Ashtavakra Gita. The line for the week is short: who am I?
screen: `JNA — TO KNOW, FROM THE INSIDE.` · `NETI, NETI: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.` · `WHO KNOWS THE KNOWER?` · `SUBTRACTION, NOT ADDITION.` · then, large: `WHO AM I?`

segments.voice: Notice the weight of your body on the seat and say inwardly, not this; then the breath, not this; then a thought passing through, not this, either. Don't push anything away; just notice it's being noticed, and rest as the one noticing, without trying to describe it. If it slips away, begin again.
Jnana yoga. The path of knowledge: not information, but knowing from the inside who you are. Its first tool is neti, neti, not this, not this.
Your line: who am I? Every answer you can point at is not quite it. Day two seventy-four.

howItsDone: In Vedanta, jnana yoga is practiced by studying the Upanishads with a teacher, reflecting on them, and meditating on the self as the witness of body and mind; 'not this, not this' (neti neti) is one of its classic tools.

original.note: Sanskrit: na iti, na iti, 'not so, not so' — Yajnavalkya's words in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

what a scholar hears: neti neti (na iti na iti) appears several times in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (e.g. 2.3.6, 3.9.26, 4.5.15); 2.4.14 asks 'by what would one know the knower?' — both central to later Advaita.
